competitors.name: iink Payments
competitors.what_they_do: Digital payments network for property insurance claim checks. Handles remote check capture, digital endorsements, multi-party disbursement and 'iink Pro', where dedicated processors handle all documents to and from the mortgage company, request servicer inspections and chase disbursements (https://help.iink.com/en/knowledge-base/what-is-a-loss-draft). Contractors who opt in can get funds advanced in 1-2 business days. Serves homeowners, contractors, public adjusters, attorneys and servicers. Pricing is $45-375/mo subscriptions, 2-3% for instant transfers, and a mortgage-processing fee of 1% of check value capped at $299-329 (https://iink.com/pricing). This overlaps the core of the idea: the draw desk, servicer chasing, inspection booking, and contractor-paid acceleration.
competitors.scale_or_funding: $12M Series A in Oct 2023 led by Headline, with Motley Fool Ventures and others (https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2023/10/19/2763431/0/en/iink-Raises-12-0MM-Series-A-to-Become-Leading-FinTech-Platform-in-Property-Insurance-Restoration.html). Also $2.8M earlier. Site claims $3B+ in checks, 120K+ checks and 30K+ stakeholders. Team of 100+. CEO says it will expand beyond payments into broader fintech for restoration pros. Holds money-transmission licensing via Avidia Bank.

competitors.name: CoPayee
competitors.what_they_do: AI tool that reads the insurance check, identifies payees, matches the servicer from a database of loss-draft forms and phone numbers, generates the servicer-specific endorsement packet and collects e-signatures. Per its FAQ it covers only the endorsement stage, not contractor draws, inspections, lien-waiver management or escalations (https://www.copayee.com/faq). Pricing is free for 1 claim, a $49 homeowner DIY kit, $199/mo Pro and $499/mo Scale. Its servicer directory is at https://www.copayee.com/mortgage-servicers.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Funding and founders not disclosed. Appears to be a very early, likely bootstrapped, AI-native tool.

competitors.name: Bankshot (Bank Shot)
competitors.what_they_do: Payments infrastructure for high-liability funds (title companies, brokerages, property managers, collections). It receives checks, wires and ACH and disburses digital or mailed checks. It publishes many loss-draft explainer articles and is listed among specialists that streamline loss-draft documentation, but the main product is generic payments rather than a homeowner rebuild desk.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Claims $561M processed across 100K+ payments via 67 partner banks. Funding not confirmed.

competitors.name: Loss-draft outsourcers to servicers (Assurant, OSC Insurance Services, Proctor Loan Protector)
competitors.what_they_do: Servicer-side vendors that run the loss-draft department itself: check endorsement and deposit, virtual inspections, call centers, tracking technology. Assurant reportedly runs the InsuranceClaimCheck.com platform for most large servicers. They sit on the other side of the counter from the homeowner, and servicers could add surge capacity or a homeowner portal through them. Also see https://proctorlp.com/service-solutions/.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established incumbents; Assurant is a public company.

competitors.name: Construction draw and lien-waiver platforms (Built, Rabbet, Land Gorilla, MightyBot, Sekady)
competitors.what_they_do: Software for construction lenders, developers and builders that automates G702/G703 draw packages, statutory lien waivers, inspections and budget checks (see https://rabbet.com/features/lien-waiver-management-software and https://landgorilla.com/construction-loan-software/). Nobody in this group serves the insurance loss-draft servicer workflow or the individual homeowner. They show the tech to assemble draw packets already exists and could be pointed at loss drafts.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Built is a well-funded construction-lending platform. Others are venture-backed. Not verified individually.

competitors.name: Public adjusters and loss-draft services (United Public Adjusters, DCS PIA, Claim Concepts, Vector Claim Solutions)
competitors.what_they_do: Public adjusters take about 10% of recovery and many advertise loss-draft and mortgage endorsement help as part of, or alongside, the claim fight (see https://www.dcspia.com/blog/insurance-claim-check-mortgage-loss-draft-texas-florida/ and https://vectorclaimsolutions.com/mortgage-endorsement-claim-check/). Some LA adjusters work pro bono on servicer disputes. They are a human substitute and could be referral partners.

competitors.name: Rebuild-side startups and nonprofits (PaliBuilds/Bidsy/ClaimArchitect, Builders Alliance, Altadena Land Initiatives gap loans, Resilient LA Delta Fund, Bank of America rebuild credit line)
competitors.what_they_do: PaliBuilds does AI bidding for 200+ contractors and challenges low insurance estimates but has no loss-draft function. Builders Alliance (https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/builders-alliance-launches-rebuild-solutions-for-los-angeles-fire-survivors-302613390.html) is a free nonprofit portal for pre-designed homes. Altadena Land Initiatives offers zero-interest gap loans through Cathay Bank (https://pasadenanow.com/main/altadena-nonprofit-launches-program-to-help-eaton-fire-survivors-bridge-rebuilding-costs). Bank of America is launching a rebuild line of credit (https://pasadenanow.com/main/bank-of-america-offers-altadena-fire-survivors-extended-mortgage-relief-rebuild-financing). None of these does servicer draw packets. They compete for the same homeowner and contractor attention, and the loans and credit line preempt the 'later bridge financing' add-on.
competitors.scale_or_funding: PaliBuilds is preparing a capital raise. The rest are nonprofit or bank programs.

white_space:
The generic layer of the idea (servicer packet preparation, chasing, inspection booking, and contractor advances) is already served. iink does it with venture funding and real scale, and CoPayee does the packet piece cheaply with AI. What the sources do not show anyone serving:
1. Homeowner-side management of total-loss, whole-house rebuilds (roughly $300K-$3M). These run over 6-18 months with permit-gated milestones, licensed-contractor verification, state-statutory conditional and unconditional lien waivers, and draw-by-draw servicer inspections. iink's pricing and deposit limits ($100K-$1M) and its subscription model are built around restoration and repair contractors, public adjusters and attorneys pushing many checks. CoPayee stops at endorsement.
2. Owner-protective verification: independent checks that milestone photos, permits and waivers match the payout requested, so the homeowner does not pay for work not done. Servicer inspectors only protect the servicer's collateral. Nothing found sells this to homeowners.
3. Regulator and executive escalation. Newsom's July 2026 directive and the DFPI complaint portal make a documented escalation dossier newly valuable, and no competitor advertises it.
4. Neutral trust position. iink and any contractor-paid model are contractor-aligned, and a homeowner advocate taking fees from contractors carries a conflict of interest.
The window is narrow. iink could add total-loss features, and regulatory pressure on servicers could shrink the pain.
evidence_of_demand:
Pain is well documented and current.
- KNX/Audacy reports mortgage companies holding Eaton and Palisades survivors' insurance money in escrow, with contractors reluctant to start. It cites 120+ complaints to the state and a public adjuster working pro bono: https://www.audacy.com/knxnews/news/local/the-latest-roadblock-eaton-and-palisade-fire-survivors-mortgage-companies
- Governor Newsom, 14 July 2026, warned lenders they are adding 'unnecessary red tape' by slowing disbursement of insurance funds during construction, and directed DFPI to collect complaints: https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/07/14/governor-newsom-warns-that-lenders-must-provide-timely-and-fair-payouts-to-la-fire-survivors/ and https://bcsa.ca.gov/newsroom/2026/07/20260716.html
- The AP story (via union-bulletin) describes survivors 'demoralized' because servicers withhold escrowed rebuild money, including moved goalposts and redundant inspections: https://www.union-bulletin.com/news/national/fire-survivors-were-finally-ready-to-rebuild-homes-a-new-barrier-is-leaving-them-demoralized/article_759b96a7-0269-5f66-b224-558f935fef77.html
- California's 2025 loss-draft laws (AB 495, 2% interest on held funds; AB 493) and the United Policyholders guide show the problem is recognized (https://uphelp.org/claim-guidance-publications/getting-your-mortgage-company-to-release-insurance-proceeds/). Servicers typically release 1/3, 1/3, 1/3 with 7-14 day inspection waits and 5-14 days added per packet correction (https://www.copayee.com/blog/how-to-get-mortgage-company-to-endorse-insurance-check).
Willingness to pay is proven, but at lower price points than the idea assumes.
- iink raised $12M and lists paid plans, with a mortgage-processing fee of 1% of check value capped at $299-329 (https://iink.com/pricing).
- CoPayee charges $49 per homeowner claim and $199-499/mo for contractors and adjusters (https://www.copayee.com/faq).
- Public adjusters take about 10%.
Caveats: no evidence found that homeowners will pay $1,500-3,000 for draw management, or that contractors will pay 1.5-2.5% per draw when iink's advance and instant-transfer fees are 2-3%. Web search budget ran out before I could check Reddit and forum threads, so direct consumer complaints beyond the news coverage are unverified.
kill_reason: n/a. Not dominated: iink is a funded direct competitor with real scale, but it targets restoration-claim check flow and does not evidently cover total-loss whole-house rebuild draw management, owner-side fraud protection or regulator escalation. It is crowded on the generic loss-draft admin and contractor-advance layer. It survives only if repositioned to the narrower wedge below.
sharper_angle:
Do not build a general loss-draft concierge, because iink and CoPayee already do the packet, chase and advance. Build the homeowner's owner's-representative for total-loss rebuilds. Concretely:
1. Serve only mortgaged total-loss rebuilds above about $300K, where the servicer requires 3-6 inspection-gated draws over 12+ months.
2. Sell independent draw verification as the product: match milestone photos, permits, contractor license and statutory lien waivers against each requested payout, and give a go/no-go recommendation. Nobody sells this to homeowners, and it also makes servicers' inspectors happier.
3. Add a regulator-ready escalation dossier (timeline, servicer commitments and misses, DFPI complaint package), timed to the July 2026 Newsom directive.
4. Drop the contractor-paid acceleration fee at the start. It conflicts with the advocate role and duplicates iink's advance. Charge the homeowner a flat success-based fee, and partner with iink or a lender for advances instead of competing on them.
5. Distribute through channels rather than ads: public adjusters (who lack this skill and would refer the second fight), Eaton Fire Survivors Network, Altadena Land Initiatives, and the free LA County and state rebuild programs.
6. Also consider a B2B2C variant: white-label surge draw capacity for servicers, who are under regulatory pressure to expand capacity. Assurant and OSC are incumbents there, so test it second.
Validate first by checking with 5 LA survivors whether they would pay $1,500+ for verification-plus-escalation, and by testing whether iink's Pro tier actually handles $500K+ multi-draw rebuilds. If it does, the wedge is thinner than it looks and the idea should be dropped.
